column5: stored food prevents death in famine
column6: The commentary connects the return of pressing after lean years with keeping valuable produce; Joseph says the stored food will sustain Egypt through seven famine years so the land will not perish, stating the life-saving purpose of the storage ordered in the preceding verse.

The commentary's pressed and stored good becomes relief when want arrives; as famine spreads, Joseph opens the storehouses and sells grain to Egyptians, bringing the preserved supply into use rather than leaving it sealed away.

column5: evil converted into preservation of life
column6: The commentary imagines pressure on a person yielding a good that others receive; Joseph tells his brothers that the evil they intended against him was turned toward preserving many lives, interpreting the outcome of his imprisonment and food administration.

The commentary locates pressing beside confinement and scarcity; Gideon beats out wheat inside a winepress to keep it from Midian, using the grape vessel as a hiding place for food under oppression rather than as a source of drink.

column5: broken cisterns unable to hold water
column6: The commentary's vessel keeps its valuable liquid from loss; Jeremiah contrasts the living-water source with cracked cisterns that cannot hold water, making a failed container an image of a people's self-inflicted deprivation.

The commentary makes renewed pressing a sign that scarcity has ended; Isaiah's judgment removes joy from the vineyards and silences the treader in the winepress, so the same action's absence signals loss.

column5: ء ن س / Hebrew אנש, table sound correspondence with BDB cognate note
column6: The commentary places the human being under pressure; Job asks what frail human is that God magnifies him and sets his attention on him, using אנוש to turn divine notice into an anguished question amid suffering.

column5: ء ن س / Aramaic אנש, table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary's al-insan is exposed to loss; Daniel sees one like a human being coming with heaven's clouds before the Ancient of Days, using the Aramaic cognate for a humanlike figure poised for a different outcome.

The surah's close calls believers to counsel one another in truth; Zechariah tells the restored community to speak truth each to the other and to render true judgments, making truthful speech a shared public practice.

column5: drink that ends thirst and becomes a spring
column6: The commentary links a dry tongue, a relieving drink and a valuable liquid kept within; Jesus says the water he gives ends thirst and becomes a spring within the recipient, turning received relief into a continuing source.

column5: outer person wastes, inner person renews
column6: The commentary places the diminished human beside a preserved inner good; Paul says the outer person is wasting away while the inner person is renewed daily, specifying what can endure inside the fragile vessel of 4:7.

The commentary says pressure may yield a valuable result beyond the loss it inflicts; Paul says momentary affliction produces an eternal weight of glory, continuing the account of pressed but uncrushed people in 4:8.

column5: wine mixed with gall offered and refused
column6: The commentary's drink can be a bitter product amid suffering; before crucifixion Jesus is offered wine mixed with gall and refuses it after tasting, so an acrid cup accompanies pressure without becoming the healing drink the commentary imagines.
The commentary calls the bitter extract a medicine; Revelation says waters made bitter by Wormwood kill many drinkers, a concrete reversal in which bitter liquid is harmful rather than curative.

The commentary's press can yield goodness for people; Revelation has an angel gather the earth's grape harvest into the great winepress of divine wrath, giving the same extraction scene a punitive end.

column5: blood flows from the trodden press
column6: The commentary treats the outflow from pressing as a possible valuable essence; Revelation's next verse says blood flows from the winepress after it is trodden, specifying a violent extract rather than a remedy.

The commentary imagines something removed under pressure so that good can emerge; Jesus says the Father prunes a fruit-bearing branch to make it bear more fruit, joining painful subtraction to a larger yield.
The surah names good deeds and reciprocal counsel; Hebrews calls hearers to consider how to stir one another to love and good works, supplying a concrete communal form for the surah's linked actions.

column5: encouraging one another as the day nears
column6: The commentary's reciprocal counsel is urgent under human loss; Hebrews asks the assembly not to abandon meeting and to encourage one another increasingly as the day approaches, adding persistence in a gathered community to the preceding call to good works.

The surah closes with believers counseling one another in patience; Paul directs the community to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak and be patient toward all, putting counsel and endurance in the same set of relations.

column5: food and drink given to an enemy
column6: The commentary interprets beneficial liquid as generosity under pressure; Paul repeats the instruction to feed a hungry enemy and give a thirsty enemy drink, carrying the concrete act from Proverbs into counsel to a Christian community.

The commentary's bitter liquid is a healing medicine; in the ordeal of jealousy the woman must drink water of bitterness that carries a curse, giving an ingested bitter fluid a punitive effect instead.

The commentary's al-insan is liable to diminution; after asking what frail humanity is, the psalm says God crowns the human with glory and honor, continuing the human scene with elevation rather than loss.

The commentary's human undergoes pressure; Job continues his question about the אנוש of 7:17 by saying God tests him every moment, making divine attention feel like sustained examination. The root itself is in the preceding verse.

The commentary's human stands under the sentence of loss; the figure described as humanlike in 7:13 receives lasting dominion and a kingdom here, completing that scene with an opposite destiny. The Aramaic אנש occurs in the preceding verse.
The commentary's vessel preserves and dispenses good under pressure; the psalmist's cup overflows at a table prepared in the presence of enemies, so contained abundance appears while threat remains.

column5: thirsty and hungry filled with good
column6: The commentary links obstructed food, thirst and a good that relieves need; the psalm says God satisfies the longing soul and fills the hungry soul with good things, bringing the two bodily lacks into one act of provision.

The surah's reciprocal counsel follows the image of pressure yielding value; Proverbs says iron sharpens iron and one person sharpens another, a specific abrasive image for mutual improvement rather than solitary patience.

column5: reward according to effort and pain
column6: The commentary proposes that a painful process can produce a valuable good; the maxim associates reward with the labor or pain expended, providing a Jewish ethical reading of effort's yield without claiming literal grape pressing.

The commentary calls patience a bitter but beneficial outcome of pressure; Hebrews says Jesus endured the cross for the joy set before him, giving a particular sufferer's ordeal and later good beside the discipline image in 12:11.

column5: cup of suffering and yielded will
column6: The commentary makes a cup and its difficult contents part of the pressured person's response; Jesus asks that the cup pass from him but submits to the Father's will, using the vessel for an ordeal faced with endurance.
The surah makes patience and counsel reciprocal under human loss; Paul tells believers to carry one another's burdens, giving shared weight a practical communal answer.

The surah joins giving counsel and sabr; Timothy is instructed to correct, rebuke and exhort with complete patience and teaching, making endurance a quality of the counsel itself, though the instruction is addressed to one teacher.

column5: good overcomes evil after water gift
column6: The commentary says a squeezed essence can become goodness given away; after directing food and drink to an enemy in 12:20, Paul says to overcome evil with good, naming the moral effect of that costly gift.

column5: fruit of vine deferred until kingdom
column6: The commentary recalls renewed pressing after a time of deprivation; Jesus says he will not drink the fruit of the vine again until drinking it new with the disciples in his Father's kingdom, setting present abstention beside future shared wine.

The commentary calls the sap named sabr a bitter medicine; this mandate presents patience as sweet and valuable in moral struggle, offering a contrary taste for the virtue. The precise subsection within Mandate 5.1 needs verification.
